title: Add AI to a website only where it helps
layout:
AI development

Add AI to a website only where it helps

Choose one visitor problem and connect the feature to a useful next step.

IN THIS ARTICLEFind a real point of frictionGive the feature a boundaryConnect to the rest of the journeyReview value after launchExample: guide a visitor to the right serviceChoose the minimum useful contextMake the normal path work without AIReview the outcome that matters

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Find a real point of friction

An AI feature should have a reason to exist beyond making the website sound modern. Consider whether visitors struggle to find the right service, understand a complex catalog or summarize a large document. If simple navigation or clearer copy resolves the problem, start there before adding another interface.

Give the feature a boundary

Define what information it uses and what it should not claim. A service assistant can help identify relevant offerings without inventing prices or promising delivery dates. Keep important business facts in a maintained source. Decide how the interface behaves when the question falls outside the available information.

Connect to the rest of the journey

The result should help the visitor take a meaningful next step: compare options, open a relevant page or prepare an inquiry. Avoid trapping useful content inside a conversation that cannot be revisited. Make the original website navigation available so users can choose a more direct path.

Review value after launch

Track whether the feature helps complete the intended task and where people abandon it. Read feedback and investigate common misunderstandings. Consider the work needed to maintain the feature, including changing content and usage controls. A small, dependable feature can be more valuable than a broad assistant that creates confusion.

Example: guide a visitor to the right service

A portfolio assistant might ask whether the visitor needs design, development or both, then direct them to a relevant service page. It can prepare a project brief based on the visitor’s answers. It should not invent a quote, claim a project has been accepted or guarantee a deadline. The final step can open a human conversation with the collected context. This gives the assistant a useful role while keeping commercial decisions with the person responsible for the work.

Choose the minimum useful context

Decide which pages or records the feature needs. A service guide may only require approved service descriptions and a few scope questions. It does not need unrestricted access to all customer communication. Keep the business content maintained in one place so the public pages and the assistant do not drift apart. When information changes, check the associated answers as well as the visible website copy.

Make the normal path work without AI

Visitors should still be able to browse services, read product details and contact the business directly. An assistant can help, but it should not become the only route to essential information. Plan a clear fallback for service interruptions. A user who cannot or does not want to interact with chat should not encounter a dead end. This also makes it easier to compare whether the AI feature adds value to the existing journey.

Review the outcome that matters

Choose a measure tied to the feature’s purpose, such as finding the correct service or preparing a sufficiently clear inquiry. Include negative outcomes: misleading answers, unnecessary steps and abandoned conversations. Inspect representative sessions with appropriate data handling. A large number of messages may indicate engagement, confusion or both. Interpret the activity in the context of the task before deciding that the feature deserves more space on the website.

KEY TAKEAWAY

Choose a measure tied to the feature’s purpose, such as finding the correct service or preparing a sufficiently clear inquiry.

title: Write AI prompts around outcomes, not magic phrases
layout:
AI development

Write AI prompts around outcomes, not magic phrases

Make the task, context and expected output clear enough to evaluate.

IN THIS ARTICLEDescribe the jobProvide constraints and examplesSeparate drafting from actionEvaluate and refineA concrete before-and-after briefUse a repeatable prompt structureDiagnose the kind of failureFinish with a reviewable output

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Describe the job

A prompt should make the intended result understandable. Instead of asking for a better website, specify the audience, the page’s purpose and the information already available. If the task is to summarize notes, say which decisions and open questions matter. Avoid including background that has no bearing on the output.

Provide constraints and examples

State the required format and any facts that must remain unchanged. An example can clarify what you mean by a concise summary or a useful category. Keep examples representative rather than idealized. If you have no evidence for a requested fact, tell the system to identify the gap instead of filling it creatively.

Separate drafting from action

A generated response and a business action have different consequences. Preparing an email draft should not automatically mean sending it. Describe which outputs need review and which data may be used. In a product, make that distinction visible through the interface rather than depending on an invisible instruction alone.

Evaluate and refine

Save a small collection of realistic inputs and compare results after changes. Look for improvements across the collection, not just one successful answer. A longer prompt is not automatically better. Remove instructions that conflict, repeat each other or do not affect the task, and keep the prompt understandable to the team maintaining it.

A concrete before-and-after brief

“Write content for my app” leaves the audience, screen and purpose unspecified. A clearer request is: draft onboarding copy for a scheduling app used by small service teams; explain that managers create shifts and employees confirm availability; use three short screens and avoid promising automatic payroll. This gives the model a task and boundaries. You can now assess whether the result explains the workflow, stays concise and avoids introducing a feature the app does not offer.

Use a repeatable prompt structure

Describe the role of the output, the facts it may rely on, the audience and the required format. Add constraints that protect the meaning, such as preserving product names or identifying missing information. Keep a place for variable input so the prompt can be reused without accidentally retaining a previous customer’s details. Version important changes with a short explanation. This makes the prompt easier for another teammate to maintain and prevents a successful one-off experiment from becoming an undocumented dependency.

Diagnose the kind of failure

An incorrect answer may come from missing context, an ambiguous instruction or an inappropriate task. Do not respond to every failure by adding more emphatic wording. If the source material lacks a delivery date, the right improvement is to surface the missing date, not to demand a more accurate guess. If the output format is inconsistent, clarify the structure and validate the result. Different failures call for different fixes.

Finish with a reviewable output

Ask for an answer the next person can inspect. For a requirements draft, separate confirmed facts, assumptions and questions. For a summary, preserve decisions and their owners. For a code task, describe the expected behavior and verification needed. Avoid requesting hidden reasoning as a substitute for evidence. A useful prompt produces an artifact that can be checked against the original task, with uncertainty visible where it affects the next decision.

KEY TAKEAWAY

Ask for an answer the next person can inspect.

title: Performance is part of the design brief
layout:
Technology

Performance is part of the design brief

Make speed a shared decision about content, media and the main user task.

IN THIS ARTICLEStart with what visitors need firstUse media with a purposeMeasure on realistic devicesKeep improvements connected to behaviorAudit the opening screenUse an image planReview movement and responsivenessBuild a maintenance habit

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Start with what visitors need first

Identify the content and controls a visitor needs to begin their task. Prioritize those elements in the experience. A dramatic introduction can become a barrier if it delays useful information. The design brief should describe the desired loading experience as well as the fully loaded page.

Source: web.dev: learn web performance ↗

Use media with a purpose

Choose images that support the content and provide appropriately sized assets. Reserve the space they will occupy so the surrounding layout remains predictable. Review whether each video, animation or embedded widget earns its cost in the experience. Visual richness is more effective when it does not compete with basic usability.

Measure on realistic devices

Do not judge performance only from a fast development computer. Consider smaller screens and less reliable connections. Look at how quickly a useful part of the page appears and whether controls respond as expected. Google’s web performance learning material provides a starting point for understanding the technical measures behind those experiences.

Keep improvements connected to behavior

Investigate the page or step where users encounter friction, then verify the change. Avoid chasing a score while ignoring a broken interaction or confusing content. Revisit performance after adding apps, media or new sections. It is a property of the evolving product, not a checkbox completed once before launch.

Audit the opening screen

List what loads before the visitor can understand the page and begin the main task. Separate essential content from optional decoration. If a large video appears before the service description, ask whether a lighter preview would communicate the same idea. Keep the visual direction intentional, but evaluate it in the context of the entire experience. A design can feel premium through typography, hierarchy and restraint as well as rich media.

Use an image plan

Decide which images need full detail and which only appear as small thumbnails. Supply dimensions and appropriate alternatives so the layout remains understandable while media loads. Avoid using a large original file for every card simply because it is available. For a gallery, prioritize the visible items and make the full view available when requested. This preserves the quality of the work without asking every visitor to load everything at once.

Review movement and responsiveness

Hover effects should provide feedback without making text difficult to read or shifting nearby controls. Continuous animation needs a way to respect reduced-motion preferences. Test a page while images are still loading and while a user interacts with it. The design should remain stable enough to use. A page that looks excellent in a still screenshot may behave poorly during the conditions visitors actually encounter.

Build a maintenance habit

Recheck important pages after adding third-party apps, new imagery or a major content section. Keep the comparison focused on the same user task and similar conditions. Where Zapier and AI fit in a business workflow

Connect the right steps and leave room for exceptions and review.

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Map the existing handoff

Zapier offers connected workflows and AI-related products including agents and chatbots. Before choosing features, describe a real process: an inquiry arrives, someone classifies it, a record is created and a teammate follows up. Mark where data moves, where judgment happens and where the process currently breaks. The product’s official overview is linked below.

Source: Zapier AI overview ↗

Separate interpretation from rules

AI can propose a category for an open-ended message. A required-field check or a known routing rule can be explicit. Treat these as different responsibilities. If the message is ambiguous, route it for review instead of forcing a classification. This makes the workflow’s decisions easier to explain to the team.

Plan for the second attempt

A connection can fail after some steps have already completed. Decide how the process recognizes an existing record before creating another one. Keep enough information to investigate a failed run without copying unnecessary personal data everywhere. A workflow is more useful when its recovery path is understandable.

Launch with a narrow pilot

Start with one inbox, one team or one record type. Review the outputs with the people who will use them, including unusual cases. Measure manual corrections and missed handoffs as well as time saved. Expand when the process is predictable, and review current integration access and pricing before committing to a production setup.

Example: route a project inquiry

An inquiry arrives with a project description and contact details. First check that the required fields exist. Then ask an AI step to suggest a service category, such as design or development, and create a draft summary for a reviewer. The reviewer confirms the category before the record is assigned. Keep the original inquiry attached to the record. This separates the customer’s words, the model’s interpretation and the team’s final decision instead of mixing them into one apparently authoritative field.

Define the record before connecting the tools

Write a simple field map: where the name comes from, where the inquiry text is stored and which identifier connects the same request across systems. Decide whether a field is required, optional or generated. Specify what should happen if a destination already contains the record. A clear field map prevents a successful-looking workflow from placing information in the wrong location. It also helps the team diagnose whether an error came from the input, the interpretation or the final handoff.

Review the quiet failures

A workflow can complete technically while still routing the wrong request. Sample completed records as well as failed runs. Check whether categories are useful to the receiving team and whether summaries omit important constraints. Let reviewers correct the outcome without needing to edit the workflow themselves. Their corrections should inform later improvements. A process that surfaces only connection failures can miss the more ordinary business errors that create confusion for customers and staff.

Choose a sensible expansion point

Expand after the team can explain how the pilot behaves and recover from its common failures. Add one meaningful variation, such as a second request type, before connecting every department. Keep a written owner and a fallback procedure for interruptions. Confirm current provider limits and access before increasing volume. This makes automation an operational improvement with clear accountability rather than an impressive diagram that only its original creator understands.

title: Designing an AI mobile app people can control

Designing an AI mobile app people can control

Keep the core task simple and make waiting, editing and recovery understandable.

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Choose an interaction that fits the task

Not every AI feature needs an open-ended chat screen. A document summary may work better as an upload, a progress state and an editable result. A conversational interface helps when the user benefits from follow-up questions. Choose the interaction based on the work rather than using chat as a default.

Use mobile constraints deliberately

Typing, reviewing and comparing large amounts of text can be difficult on a small screen. Offer focused starting actions and clear output sections. Keep the original input accessible without overwhelming the result. Avoid requiring users to remember information from several screens while deciding whether a generated answer is useful.

Explain waiting and failure

Show that a request has started and let users stop or retry when appropriate. If a request fails, retain the input so the user does not have to recreate it. Distinguish an unavailable service from a task that the product does not support. The recovery message should tell people what they can do next.

Keep users in charge

Make editing, dismissing and reporting a result straightforward. Ask before actions that send, publish or change important records. Evaluate the experience with imperfect outputs as well as successful ones. A trustworthy AI app is not one that pretends mistakes never happen; it helps the user recognize and recover from them.

A practical screen sequence

For a document assistant, a coherent first version can include an input screen, a processing state, an editable result and a saved-history view. Define what happens if the user leaves while processing. Decide whether the result is saved automatically or only after confirmation, and communicate that choice. Keep the primary action visible without covering important content. This sequence is more useful to a development team than a single beautiful chat screenshot that leaves persistence and recovery undefined.

Make generated text easy to inspect

Break long results into meaningful sections and let users return to the source. Avoid presenting every sentence as equally important. If the task produces action items, distinguish suggested actions from completed ones. Use clear controls for copying or exporting and confirm what was copied. For a small screen, predictable text structure often contributes more to usability than decorative bubbles, animated avatars or a large collection of preset prompts.

Test the interruptions deliberately

Try a slow request, a lost connection, a rejected upload and a user switching apps midway through the task. Check whether the input remains available and whether returning creates duplicate requests. Ask the developer to define which operations can be canceled and which continue in the background. The interface should reflect those decisions accurately. Do not show a cancel control if it merely hides progress while the important operation continues unchanged.

Release a bounded feature

Start with a task that users can evaluate and a clear feedback route. Keep a record of common corrections without collecting unnecessary private content. Review whether the feature helps people finish the intended job. If users repeatedly abandon the generated result, investigate whether the task, input or presentation is wrong before adding another AI capability. A focused app can improve over time when the team understands what its first feature is actually doing.

Start with a task that users can evaluate and a clear feedback route.

title: A learning app should make progress understandable

A learning app should make progress understandable

Help learners choose a next step and return without losing context.

IN THIS ARTICLEDefine the learning journeyOrganize lessons into useful unitsGive feedback that teachesDesign for interruptionsExample: a learner returns after a weekAlign the interface with the learning taskHandle AI assistance carefullyReview progress with educators and learners

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Define the learning journey

Identify the intended learner and the task they want to accomplish. A course catalog, a practice tool and a reference library serve different needs. Decide what an appropriate next step looks like for a new learner and for someone returning. The opening screen should reflect that difference instead of treating every visit as a fresh start.

Organize lessons into useful units

Make lesson titles describe what the learner will work on. Show prerequisites and an approximate commitment where useful. Allow people to resume without searching through the entire course. Progress indicators should reflect meaningful completion rather than merely rewarding a page visit or a tap.

Give feedback that teaches

When a learner makes a mistake, explain the relevant idea and provide a way to try again. A red indicator with no explanation communicates failure without helping learning. For open-ended work, clarify how it will be reviewed. Avoid presenting an automated response as a definitive assessment when the task needs human judgment.

Design for interruptions

People learn between other responsibilities. Preserve their place and make it clear what remains unfinished. Consider short sessions, unstable connections and readable content on small screens. Measure whether people can continue a useful learning task, not just whether they open the app frequently or accumulate decorative badges.

Example: a learner returns after a week

The learner should see the course they were using, the last completed lesson and a clear way to continue. Offer enough context to remember the topic without forcing a complete restart. If an exercise was left unfinished, make its state visible. A streak or badge may be secondary information, but it should not replace the practical answer to “What should I do next?” on the opening screen.

Align the interface with the learning task

Reading an explanation, practicing a skill and reviewing feedback are different activities. Give each an appropriate layout and clear transition. A lesson page may need focused content and progress, while a practice screen may need room for an answer and feedback. Avoid adding unnecessary navigation during a task that requires concentration. Ask whether each control supports learning or merely makes the screen appear busier.

Handle AI assistance carefully

If an AI helper is included, define whether it explains concepts, gives hints or evaluates answers. Those roles should be clear to the learner. Avoid giving away an answer when the goal is practice, and avoid presenting uncertain feedback as a definitive grade. Let learners report confusing guidance and return to the source material. The helper should support the learning design rather than becoming an unrelated chat feature attached to the course.

Review progress with educators and learners

Test whether progress labels reflect meaningful work. A learner who opened every lesson has not necessarily understood the material. Discuss what completion means for the particular course and how feedback should influence the next activity. Include people returning after interruptions, not only motivated first-time users. A useful learning product supports the ordinary pattern of starting, stopping, reviewing and continuing.

title: What your website’s backend actually does

What your website’s backend actually does

Understand the responsibilities behind a polished interface before scoping a build.

IN THIS ARTICLESeparate presentation from decisionsThink in complete requestsExpect imperfect connectionsScope the operating workExample: reserving an appointmentDefine the contract between teamsKeep trusted decisions on the trusted sideAsk useful handoff questions

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Separate presentation from decisions

The interface displays information and collects input. The backend can handle trusted operations such as checking access, updating stored records and coordinating integrations. The exact division depends on the product. A static portfolio may need very little server behavior; a multi-user operations platform needs much more.

Source: MDN: server-side website programming ↗

Think in complete requests

For a booking action, consider the whole sequence: input validation, availability, authorization, record creation and a response. Define what happens when something changes during the request. A successful screen design does not automatically answer those questions. They should be part of the discussion between design and development.

Expect imperfect connections

Requests can fail, arrive late or be repeated. Give the interface meaningful loading, error and retry behavior. Preserve user input when recovery is possible. For important actions, the team should agree on how the system avoids duplicate effects and how it communicates the final state to the user.

Scope the operating work

Discuss hosting, access management, backups, monitoring and who responds to failures. These responsibilities affect the product beyond its first release. A useful development proposal names the required integrations and the assumptions around them. This helps the client distinguish a visual prototype from a functioning service with ongoing responsibilities.

Example: reserving an appointment

A visitor chooses an available time and submits a booking request. The backend needs to confirm that the time is still available before storing the reservation. It should return a result the interface can explain, such as confirmed or no longer available. Two people may request the same slot close together. Planning this situation helps the team avoid a design that assumes every visible option remains available indefinitely.

Define the contract between teams

Agree on the information sent with a request and the possible responses. Describe required fields, validation errors and permission failures in a way both frontend and backend developers can use. Include example responses when useful. A clear contract allows the interface to handle expected states before the integration is finished and makes it easier to identify whether an issue comes from the client, the service or the data.

Keep trusted decisions on the trusted side

A browser can display a price or hide an action, but those interface choices do not establish authorization. The backend should check the rules relevant to the operation. Discuss ownership of records and access between different customers early. A polished admin page can still be incomplete if the corresponding service accepts actions from people who should not be able to perform them.

Ask useful handoff questions

Who maintains the service, how are configuration changes managed and what happens when an integration is unavailable? What information helps support investigate a failed request? Which responsibilities belong to the client and which belong to the developer? These questions make an estimate more concrete. They also help distinguish a clickable demonstration, a test deployment and a service prepared for real users.

title: Using Perplexity as a starting point for research
layout:

Using Perplexity as a starting point for research

Follow the sources, separate evidence from interpretation and keep useful notes.

IN THIS ARTICLEBegin with an answerable questionRead beyond the summaryKeep facts and judgments separateTurn findings into a decisionExample: compare three competing servicesCreate an evidence tableHandle disagreements between sourcesTurn the research into a design question

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Begin with an answerable question

Perplexity presents search-based answers with links to sources. A narrow research question is easier to verify than a broad request for everything about a market. Define the audience, time period and decision you are trying to make. The official introduction linked below explains the product’s core approach.

Source: What is Perplexity? ↗

Read beyond the summary

Open the linked material that supports an important claim. Check whether it actually addresses the question, when it was published and whether the author is reporting evidence or offering an opinion. A citation is a route to verification; its presence alone does not mean the statement is settled.

Keep facts and judgments separate

In your notes, distinguish a sourced statement from your interpretation of it. For a product brief, a competitor’s published feature is evidence about that product. Your belief that users need the same feature is a hypothesis. Keeping those separate prevents research summaries from quietly turning assumptions into requirements.

Turn findings into a decision

End the research session with a short comparison of options and the uncertainty that remains. Save the source links that matter so someone else can check them. Avoid gathering more material without a purpose. A useful research output should help the team choose what to investigate, design or test next.

Example: compare three competing services

Begin with a question such as which onboarding steps three named products require for a new team. Use research to locate the relevant official pages, then record the steps with links and dates. Do not translate a feature list into a claim about usability without observing the experience. A product may advertise a capability while placing it behind a particular plan or configuration. Mark those uncertainties instead of filling the gaps with the most plausible interpretation.

Create an evidence table

Keep one row per claim, with the supporting page, the date checked and the implication for your project. Use a separate column for unresolved questions. For example, an official page may confirm that a product supports invited teammates, but not explain whether an invitation can be revoked. That distinction directs the next research step. The table is useful because another person can follow the evidence without recreating your entire search session or trusting an uncited summary.

Handle disagreements between sources

When sources conflict, look for differences in publication date, audience, region or product version. Prefer a directly relevant primary source for a product’s documented behavior. If the conflict remains unresolved, say so in your notes and avoid building a critical requirement on that claim. Research does not need to erase uncertainty to be useful. It should make the uncertainty visible enough for the team to decide whether further investigation is worth the effort.

Turn the research into a design question

End with a small number of questions to test, not a list of competitor features to copy. If several products use a long setup form, ask whether your users need all those fields before they can get value. The observed pattern is evidence of what those products do; it is not proof that the pattern is right for your audience. This distinction keeps competitive research connected to product judgment rather than imitation.

Start with the products

Shopify offers themes with different layouts and customization options. Before selecting one, understand the catalog: a small focused range and a large multi-category store need different browsing experiences. List the information customers need to compare products. Use those requirements to evaluate themes instead of choosing from the homepage screenshot alone.

Source: Shopify themes documentation ↗

Inspect the product journey

Review collection pages, product detail and the path to the cart. Try long titles, multiple variants and realistic descriptions. Check how the same content behaves on mobile. A theme should support the customer’s decisions without requiring a large amount of custom work to handle your everyday catalog.

Separate styling from functionality

Write down what the theme supports and what may require customization or an app. Clarify the effort and any recurring costs before committing. A visual reference does not guarantee that a theme includes the underlying behavior. Agree on which parts of the reference matter most to your store.

Test with real content

Use representative products and images before finalizing the direction. Review the desktop and mobile homepage together with at least one product page. This gives everyone a more accurate picture of the store than a polished placeholder demo. Record the approved direction so the remaining build follows the same decisions.

Create a shortlist from requirements

List the browsing patterns and product information the store needs, then compare a small number of themes against that list. For example, a clothing catalog may depend on variant selection and sizing information, while a focused product brand may need strong product storytelling. Treat visual style as one criterion alongside content fit and customization effort. A popular theme is not automatically the best starting point for a particular catalog.

Use a representative product page

Choose a product with realistic complexity, not the simplest item in the store. Include a long description, several images and the variants customers actually select. Review what appears before the primary action on a phone. Check whether supporting information is discoverable without overwhelming the page. This review reveals practical differences between themes that may look similar in a clean demonstration with perfectly sized content.

Record what requires extra work

Separate theme configuration, custom design, custom development and third-party functionality in the proposal. Describe which behavior is included in the agreed scope. If an app is being considered, confirm current compatibility, cost and responsibilities before installation. Do not imply that buying a theme automatically delivers every interaction shown in an unrelated reference. A clear distinction here prevents disagreements later about what the theme purchase covered.

Approve a direction, not just a screenshot

Review the homepage, collection page and representative product page on desktop and mobile. Agree on typography, spacing, image treatment and navigation. Include realistic content and note anything still awaiting final assets. Once the direction is approved, use it consistently across the remaining pages. The decision should give the team a reusable set of rules, not a single attractive frame that leaves the rest of the store open to interpretation.

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Capture what the team needs

A useful inquiry form asks enough to route the request without becoming an interview. Collect the person’s preferred contact details, the type of project and a short description. Explain what happens next. Avoid collecting fields simply because they might be interesting later; every extra field adds effort.

Define ownership and status

Agree on who handles each type of inquiry and what the statuses mean. New, in review and contacted should describe observable steps. If everyone assumes someone else owns the request, automation will only move that ambiguity between tools. Make the next responsible person visible in the record.

Use AI as a suggestion layer

For an open-ended brief, AI may propose a category or prepare a summary. Keep the original message available and let a person correct the suggestion. Do not let a generated summary silently replace the customer’s actual request. Important commitments, such as pricing or delivery dates, still need an authorized decision.

Design the exceptions

Decide how duplicates, missing information and failed connections appear to the team. Maintain a review queue for requests that cannot be routed confidently. Measure missed inquiries and time to meaningful follow-up, not just the number of automated steps. The purpose is a more reliable conversation with the prospective customer.

A sample intake-to-handoff process

A visitor submits an inquiry, the system checks required fields and a reviewer confirms the service category. The inquiry receives an owner and a visible next step. A prepared response may acknowledge receipt, but a quote is created only after scope review. Keep the status changes connected to actual actions. A request should not become “contacted” simply because a draft was generated, and it should not become “qualified” because the form was complete.

Decide how similar inquiries are handled

The same person may submit a revised brief or contact you through several channels. Choose an approach for linking related inquiries without discarding the newer message. Show the reviewer why the system thinks the records belong together. Avoid automatically merging solely because two names match. The objective is to preserve the conversation’s context while reducing duplicate follow-up, not to produce an artificially clean database that hides important changes.

Give staff a useful exception queue

A queue should show why a request needs attention, how long it has been waiting and who can resolve it. Missing contact information and a failed integration need different responses. Let staff record the resolution and continue the workflow without recreating the entire inquiry. Review whether recurring exceptions indicate an unclear form, an unsuitable rule or a real variation in the business process.

Measure the human outcome

Track whether customers receive a relevant response and whether the assigned teammate has enough information to act. Review a small sample of completed handoffs each week during the pilot. Ask staff which summaries they rewrite and which fields they ignore. Remove automation that adds noise without helping the next person. The process is successful when fewer inquiries are lost and conversations begin with better context, not when every possible step has an AI label.

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Choose the questions it should answer

Start with a defined knowledge area, such as product setup or internal onboarding. List common questions and identify where authoritative answers live. A chatbot cannot compensate for contradictory instructions or missing policies. Assign an owner to keep the underlying material current before expecting reliable responses from it.

Design for evidence

When an answer relies on a document, give users a way to inspect the relevant source. Separate a direct statement from an interpretation. If the available material does not support an answer, the assistant should say so and offer a next step. Confident language is not a substitute for evidence.

Respect access boundaries

A user should only receive information they are entitled to see. Consider permissions when selecting source material and when presenting results. A visually hidden document is not necessarily inaccessible to the backend. Discuss the authorization model with the development team, especially when several customer organizations share the same product.

Include a human path

Make escalation easy and preserve enough context to avoid asking the customer to repeat everything. Collect feedback on wrong or incomplete answers. Review a sample of real questions after release and update the content or workflow accordingly. The launch is the beginning of maintaining the service, not the end of the work.

Prepare the content before the interface

Review a small set of authoritative documents for contradictions, obsolete steps and unclear ownership. Give each document a useful title and a reason to exist. If two pages describe different versions of the same process, make the applicable version explicit. A chatbot that searches inconsistent material inherits that inconsistency. Improving the source content often helps both the assistant and the people who prefer to read the documentation directly.

Example: answer a product setup question

A customer asks how to invite a teammate. The assistant should find the relevant setup instructions, explain the supported steps and link to the source. If the customer’s role cannot send invitations, the response should describe the appropriate next step rather than repeating a button they cannot access. If the available documentation does not cover their plan, the assistant should acknowledge that gap. This keeps the response connected to the user’s actual situation.

Evaluate access and unsupported requests

Test questions whose answers are in the knowledge base, questions that require several documents and questions that cannot be answered from it. Include attempts to obtain information belonging to another team. Confirm that authorization is enforced by the application’s data access layer. Do not rely only on an instruction telling the model to behave. Review generated answers for unsupported details, misleading certainty and links that do not support the associated claim.

Build a maintenance loop

Assign a content owner and a review schedule for recurring unanswered questions. A missing answer may require a new document, a clearer product feature or a handoff to support. Keep those options distinct instead of trying to solve every issue with prompt changes. Review the assistant after significant product updates. Track whether users reach the correct next step, including successful escalation, rather than treating every conversation without a human response as a success.

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Define the expected information

List the fields your process needs and where they will be used. A document intake workflow might need a reference number, date and request category. Establish validation rules for each field. If different document types need different information, identify the type before forcing everything into a single structure.

Keep the original accessible

Reviewers should be able to compare extracted values against the source document. Show which fields are missing or ambiguous instead of displaying an incomplete record as finished. A correction should preserve enough context for someone to understand what changed. This is particularly useful when documents arrive in inconsistent formats.

Separate extraction from approval

Reading a value does not establish that it is correct or authorized. Treat extraction, validation and approval as distinct steps. A completed review can trigger the next action. Avoid designing a workflow where an uncertain interpretation immediately changes an important record with no opportunity for correction.

Plan for repeated submissions

A file may be uploaded twice, replaced by a revised version or retried after a failure. Agree on how the workflow identifies those situations. Give the team a clear way to reopen a record when needed. Judge the system by completed, accurate handoffs rather than the volume of files it can ingest.

Example: process a service request form

A team receives completed request documents with different layouts. The workflow identifies the document type, extracts a reference number and requested service, and places uncertain fields in a review state. A staff member compares them with the original and confirms the record. Only then does the request enter the normal work queue. This separates reading a document from approving its contents and makes the reviewer’s responsibility visible.

Design a side-by-side review screen

Place the source document near the extracted values and highlight the field currently being checked. Let reviewers correct a value without losing their place. Distinguish a missing field from an unreadable one because the next action may differ. Preserve meaningful changes in the record history. For a longer document, provide a reference to the relevant page rather than expecting reviewers to search the entire file for every value.

Handle versions without confusion

A customer may send a corrected form after the first version was reviewed. Decide whether that creates a new request or updates the existing one, and show which version is active. Retain enough history to understand previous decisions. A replacement should not silently overwrite a value that has already triggered downstream work. Identify which changes require another approval before the process continues.

Set a realistic definition of completion

A file is not complete merely because extraction ran successfully. Completion might require validated fields, an assigned owner and confirmation that the destination received the record. Track those states separately. Review how often people correct extracted values and why. The results can guide improvements to the intake form, source document template or review interface, rather than assuming a different AI model is the answer to every operational problem.

When does your product need a design system?

Recognize the point where reusable patterns become more valuable than one-off screens.

IN THIS ARTICLELook for repeated decisionsDefine behavior as well as appearanceKeep design and code connectedStart small and maintain itAudit the patterns already in useExample: define one form field properlyChoose an ownership modelMeasure usefulness through adoption

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Look for repeated decisions

If your team keeps recreating buttons, form fields or spacing rules, a small component system can help. Start with the patterns already appearing in your product instead of inventing a large library.

Define behavior as well as appearance

A button needs focus, disabled and loading behavior. A field needs a label, helpful feedback and an error state. A useful design system describes these decisions, not just the default screen.

Keep design and code connected

Components in Figma and components in code should use a shared vocabulary. Discuss how variants map between the two and who maintains them when the product changes.

Start small and maintain it

Choose a few widely used components, document their purpose and refine them through real use. A modest system that the team trusts is more useful than a huge one nobody maintains.

Audit the patterns already in use

Collect examples of buttons, inputs, navigation, cards and feedback messages from the current product. Group similar patterns and identify differences that have a meaningful purpose. Some variation may be necessary, while other variation may reflect accidental duplication. Start the system with the most widely used decisions. A small set of clear components usually contributes more than an impressive catalog built before the product’s needs are understood.

Example: define one form field properly

Specify the label, input, helper text and error message together. Include empty, filled, focused, disabled and invalid states where relevant. Explain when each state should appear and how the field behaves with long content. Coordinate the design with its code implementation. This turns the component into a reusable interaction rather than a picture of the default state, and it reduces the need for each feature team to make the same decisions again.

Choose an ownership model

Name the people who review proposed changes and how product teams request a new pattern. Keep the process proportionate to the team’s size. A small team may need a shared review rather than a formal committee. Document the reason for important decisions so someone can judge whether a future exception is justified. Without ownership, the system may drift into several competing versions even if its initial design was carefully prepared.

Measure usefulness through adoption

Watch whether teams can use the components in real features without repeatedly detaching or rebuilding them. Ask where documentation is missing and which variants cause confusion. Update the system from those observations. Avoid treating the number of components as a measure of success. The system is useful when it helps people create coherent interfaces with less repeated decision-making and when it remains understandable as the product grows.

GitHub Copilot: keep the review in the workflow

How to use an AI coding assistant without confusing generated code with finished work.

IN THIS ARTICLEUnderstand the assistant’s roleGive the task useful boundariesReview behavior, not just syntaxKeep accountability explicitExample: improve a checkout error stateKeep the proposed change small enough to inspectAvoid a circular definition of correctnessA useful team agreement

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Understand the assistant’s role

GitHub describes Copilot as an assistant for writing, understanding and reviewing software, with features that depend on the plan and environment. A useful starting point is a bounded change with a clear acceptance condition. Ask for an explanation of an unfamiliar function or a focused improvement before handing over a broad feature.

Source: About GitHub Copilot ↗

Give the task useful boundaries

Specify the expected behavior, the files involved and any conventions that should remain intact. For example, a form improvement might need accessible labels, server-side validation and an existing error component. Clear constraints reduce the number of plausible but inappropriate solutions. Do not assume the assistant knows decisions that only exist in someone’s head.

Review behavior, not just syntax

Readable code can still do the wrong thing. Check empty input, failed requests and the effect on existing users. For a permissions change, inspect the server-side decision rather than relying on a hidden button. Use tests where they provide meaningful evidence about the risk of the change.

Keep accountability explicit

Someone should understand and own the code that reaches production. Record why a change was made, review dependencies and confirm that any suggested API matches the project. The value of an assistant is easier to assess when you track the complete task, including review and corrections, rather than only the time spent producing a first draft.

Example: improve a checkout error state

Suppose a checkout form currently shows the same error for every failure. A focused task is to distinguish missing input, a declined request and an unavailable service while preserving entered information. Supply the existing component and explain which behavior must remain unchanged. Ask the assistant to describe its intended change before editing. Review the resulting behavior against those requirements, including a retry after a failed request. A more elegant implementation is not sufficient if customers still lose their form data.

Keep the proposed change small enough to inspect

Separate an error-state fix from an unrelated component rewrite. If an assistant changes naming, formatting, dependencies and business logic together, reviewers must examine several kinds of risk at once. Request a narrower patch when necessary. Read the final difference rather than only the assistant’s summary of it. The summary can help navigation, but the actual changed files are the evidence. Preserve the reasoning behind important choices in a short review note.

Avoid a circular definition of correctness

A test generated from the same mistaken assumption as the implementation may simply confirm that both share the mistake. Start with observable acceptance conditions written independently of the suggested code. For the checkout example, entering valid details after a failure should still work, and refreshing must not silently duplicate an order. Select verification appropriate to the action’s consequences. A text change needs less scrutiny than a payment or authorization change.

A useful team agreement

Decide what an assistant may prepare and what a person must approve. The agreement can cover dependency additions, production configuration and access to sensitive files without banning ordinary assistance. Use repository conventions to reduce repeated corrections. During a retrospective, ask whether the tool reduced the complete delivery effort, including review and repair. Teams learn more from that question than from counting generated lines, accepted suggestions or how quickly the first patch appeared.

Using Figma AI without skipping the design thinking

Generated starting points still need clear goals, review and a consistent system.

IN THIS ARTICLEStart with the problemUse a brief with constraintsInspect the interaction statesKeep the handoff understandableExample: generate a starting point for onboardingCritique with realistic contentMove useful patterns into the systemKnow when to stop generating

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Start with the problem

Figma offers AI features within its design product family. The official product page describes the available capabilities, which may change over time. Before exploring them, write down the user’s task and the information the screen must communicate. A visually polished starting point is useful only if it helps that task.

Source: Figma AI overview ↗

Use a brief with constraints

Include the audience, content hierarchy, required states and existing components. For a booking screen, that could mean location, date, availability and a clear confirmation state. Constraints make alternatives easier to compare. Without them, you may spend time choosing between attractive layouts that all miss an important requirement.

Inspect the interaction states

Review what happens when content is long, a list is empty or an action fails. Check whether components fit the design system and whether text remains readable on smaller screens. AI-assisted work still benefits from the same design critique as a manually assembled interface. It should not receive an automatic pass because it was generated quickly.

Keep the handoff understandable

Name the components, document significant decisions and confirm behavior with the developer. Remove exploratory elements that no longer belong in the final design. The deliverable should communicate a coherent product direction, not the history of every generated variation. Evaluate the tool by the quality and clarity of the completed workflow.

Example: generate a starting point for onboarding

Describe the audience, the information already known and the first useful task after signup. Ask for a short onboarding flow that collects only what the product needs to begin. Review each field by asking what decision it enables. If removing a field does not affect the next task, consider collecting it later. Use the generated layout to make these tradeoffs concrete, rather than treating a polished first result as the final answer.

Critique with realistic content

Replace sample names, perfect headings and evenly sized descriptions with content that resembles the real product. Try a long company name, an untranslated label and a missing profile image. These examples reveal whether the visual system handles variation. Review keyboard navigation and error placement with the developer rather than assuming the design tool has resolved implementation details. A useful critique identifies a specific decision to improve, not simply whether the screen looks modern.

Move useful patterns into the system

Identify repeated controls and compare them with existing components. Reuse a suitable pattern before creating another almost-identical variation. Document meaningful differences, such as a destructive action or a loading state. Keep experiments outside the approved handoff frames so the team can distinguish exploration from the current decision. The goal is a product that feels consistent across screens, even when different tools helped create those screens.

Know when to stop generating

If new variations keep changing decoration without improving the task, return to the brief. Write down the unresolved question and seek evidence from content, users or technical constraints. More generated alternatives will not settle a missing business decision. Finish with an approved flow, representative states and a short explanation of key choices. That package helps development far more than a large collection of visually different screens with no clear direction.

title: Design an e-commerce app around confident decisions
layout:

Design an e-commerce app around confident decisions

Make products easy to understand and the next step easy to find.

IN THIS ARTICLESupport discovery without overloadMake product detail do the workKeep the cart understandableDesign after the orderExample: selecting a product variantCreate a usable filter experienceReview the order summary carefullyTest with a realistic purchase task

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Support discovery without overload

Organize categories using language customers understand. Give search and filtering a clear purpose, especially when the catalog is large. Avoid placing every promotion ahead of the products. A useful browse screen helps people narrow the choice rather than requiring them to decode the business’s internal organization.

Make product detail do the work

Customers need more than a picture and a purchase button. Show the information that affects the decision, including variants, availability and the details relevant to the product. Keep the selected option visible. If a required choice is missing, explain it next to the control instead of returning a vague error.

Keep the cart understandable

Reflect what has been selected and make quantity changes clear. Explain when the total changes and surface important additional charges before the final decision. Preserve the cart when the user leaves to check a product detail. A purchase flow should not punish a person for double-checking an important choice.

Design after the order

An order confirmation should describe what happens next and where the customer can find help. Consider delayed, canceled and partially fulfilled orders in the product scope. The experience continues after payment. Reviewing those states early helps the development team build a more complete service rather than only a successful checkout demonstration.

Example: selecting a product variant

A shopper opens a product that comes in several sizes and colors. Keep the available choices clear and show the selected combination near the purchase action. If one combination is unavailable, explain that state at the relevant choice. Do not wait until the final step to reveal the problem. If a shopper changes color after selecting size, make it clear whether the size remains valid or needs to be selected again.

Create a usable filter experience

Choose filters based on meaningful product differences and show the active choices when the user returns to the results. Let people clear one filter without losing all the others. Distinguish no matching products from an empty catalog. On mobile, preserve the browsing position when opening and closing a product. These small decisions reduce repeated work and help shoppers compare options without feeling that the app resets after every action.

Review the order summary carefully

The final review should make the selected items, quantities and relevant charges understandable. Use the same product names and options throughout the journey. If a value changes, explain why before the user commits. Consider what happens when an item becomes unavailable or a request fails. The app should preserve enough information for a sensible retry and communicate whether the order was actually created.

Test with a realistic purchase task

Give a participant a specific need and ask them to find a suitable item, compare alternatives and complete the intended flow in a test environment. Watch where they hesitate and what information they seek. Avoid directing them to the correct control. Their behavior can reveal unclear labels, missing product details and unnecessary steps. Use those findings to improve the journey before focusing on decorative interactions.

Give a participant a specific need and ask them to find a suitable item, compare alternatives and complete the intended flow in a test environment.

title: What to include in a Shopify development brief
layout:

What to include in a Shopify development brief

Help your designer and developer estimate the actual store, not an imagined one.

IN THIS ARTICLEDescribe the catalog and audienceList the important journeysAgree on design review pointsMake ownership and costs explicitBuild a simple page-and-function mapSeparate approved content from placeholdersAgree on the release checklistKeep changes reviewable

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Describe the catalog and audience

Explain what you sell, who buys it and how people choose between products. Include the number of initial products and any meaningful variation in their content. If some photography or copy is unfinished, say so. The team can then plan placeholders without mistaking them for approved launch content.

List the important journeys

Describe the pages and actions customers need. A store might include collection browsing, product comparison, subscriptions or a wholesale inquiry flow. Do not assume a short phrase such as standard e-commerce captures every requirement. Clarify which journeys are essential for the first release and which can come later.

Agree on design review points

Review the homepage and a representative product page before building the full store. Include mobile layouts and the main typography and color decisions. This catches disagreements while the work is still focused. After approval, new directions should be discussed as scope changes rather than hidden inside routine revisions.

Make ownership and costs explicit

Specify who supplies the theme, domain, product content and required app accounts. Ask for additional or recurring costs to be identified before installation. Define the handoff and the launch checklist. A clear brief does not remove every unknown, but it makes the project’s assumptions visible before they become expensive surprises.

Build a simple page-and-function map

For every required page, write its purpose, primary content and main action. A collection page helps shoppers narrow options; a product page helps them decide; an FAQ answers recurring concerns. Then list functions that affect several pages, such as account access or a particular catalog rule. This keeps the brief from becoming a mixture of page names, visual preferences and technical features with no clear relationship between them.

Separate approved content from placeholders

Label product photography, reviews, claims and descriptions according to their status. A placeholder helps the design continue, but it should not be mistaken for publishable content. Assign an owner to replace each unfinished item and define the final review point. In particular, do not use invented reviews or unsupported product claims to make the demo look complete. The layout can demonstrate where verified material will appear without pretending that material already exists.

Agree on the release checklist

Describe what the team will verify before launch, including the shopping journey, navigation, required content and agreed integrations. Confirm who makes the final go-live decision and who owns the store accounts. Use a written list so both sides know what remains. Avoid treating the last visual review as proof that every operational setting has been checked; storefront appearance and store readiness are different parts of the handoff.

Keep changes reviewable

When a new request appears, compare it with the agreed scope and explain its effect before implementing it. A small content edit and a new shopping workflow are not the same kind of change. Record approved adjustments in a place both sides can access. Clear change handling protects the relationship because the client can make an informed choice about priorities instead of discovering extra work or a delayed timeline at the end.

When a new request appears, compare it with the agreed scope and explain its effect before implementing it.

Design admin panels around decisions and permissions

The useful dashboard is the one that helps someone complete the next task.

IN THIS ARTICLEBegin with the workMake table states clearTreat permission as a system ruleInclude a traceable historyExample: separate support from administrationDesign an action with consequencesMake the dashboard answer a questionReview the complete role journey

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Begin with the work

Ask what each role needs to inspect, decide or change. An operations manager may need an exception queue before a large chart. A support agent may need a record’s history and the next allowed action. Organize the interface around these tasks instead of filling the opening screen with unrelated totals.

Make table states clear

Tables need useful column labels, filters and understandable empty states. Distinguish no records from no results for the current filters. Preserve enough context when opening a detail view so users can return to their place. A busy operational screen should reduce repeated searching, not make people memorize rows.

Treat permission as a system rule

The interface can explain which actions are available, but the server must enforce access. Discuss permissions at the record and action level rather than assuming one admin role is sufficient. For an important change, show the affected record and consequence before the user confirms it.

Include a traceable history

Decide which changes need a history and who may inspect it. Show timestamps and actors in a way the team can interpret. Avoid exposing unrelated personal information in an activity feed. Test the dashboard using the least privileged role as well as the administrator; both are part of the real product experience.

Example: separate support from administration

A support agent may need to view an order and add a note, while a manager may approve a refund and an administrator may change access. Model those actions separately. The interface should show the relevant information for each task and explain when escalation is required. Avoid giving everyone broad access simply because the first version has few users. It is easier to discuss the intended responsibilities before workflows become dependent on unrestricted permissions.

Design an action with consequences

For an important change, show the affected record and the expected effect before confirmation. If several records are selected, show how many are included and whether any are excluded. Provide a clear result after the action, including partial failures. An ambiguous success message creates extra checking work. Where undo is supported, explain its limits so users do not assume every action can be reversed later.

Make the dashboard answer a question

Choose a small number of measures that lead to decisions. An overdue-work count should connect to the records that need attention. A trend should have a meaningful time period and a clear definition. Avoid combining unrelated numbers merely to fill a grid. Ask users what they would do differently after seeing each metric. If there is no answer, the metric may belong in a report rather than the main operational screen.

Review the complete role journey

Test the product as a restricted user from entry to completion. Include direct requests to protected operations, not only clicking visible buttons. Confirm that the history records meaningful changes and that error messages do not expose unrelated information. During handoff, explain the role model in ordinary terms. The team should understand who can do what, how access is granted and who is responsible for reviewing it.

Test the product as a restricted user from entry to completion.

title: A food delivery app is more than a menu
layout:

A food delivery app is more than a menu

Plan the customer journey together with the restaurant and delivery workflows.

IN THIS ARTICLEBegin with availabilityMake customization predictableConnect the status to real operationsInclude every role in scopeMap the order across all participantsExample: an item becomes unavailableTreat location and timing as live informationPrepare a focused first release

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Begin with availability

Customers need to know whether the service can deliver to their location and whether a restaurant is accepting orders. Ask for the information necessary to answer those questions without creating unnecessary friction. Explain an unavailable area or closed restaurant clearly, and give a useful alternative when one exists.

Make customization predictable

Meal options, required selections and additional charges should be understandable before the item enters the cart. Distinguish an optional note from a supported customization. Show how the order changes when an option is selected. The restaurant should receive an unambiguous version of what the customer intended to request.

Connect the status to real operations

Accepted, preparing, collected and delivered should correspond to actual updates in the service. Do not show reassuring progress that the system cannot verify. Define what happens when the restaurant rejects an item, a courier is delayed or a customer cannot be reached. These are ordinary product states, not unusual afterthoughts.

Include every role in scope

The customer app is only one part of the product. Discuss restaurant handling, dispatch, customer support and administrative tools during planning. Identify where staff need to intervene and what information they should see. A well-designed ordering screen cannot make up for missing workflows behind the order.

Map the order across all participants

Write down what the customer, restaurant, delivery team and support staff see at each stage. A customer’s confirmed order needs a corresponding restaurant task. A rejected item needs a resolution, not just a notification. Mark where one participant is waiting for another. This reveals missing handoffs that are easy to overlook when the design process focuses only on the customer’s screens.

Example: an item becomes unavailable

The restaurant discovers an ordered item is unavailable. Decide whether staff can propose a replacement, remove the item or cancel the order, and whether the customer must approve the change. Show the revised order clearly before continuing. The interface should not silently substitute a different meal. This scenario affects notifications, order status, support tools and the customer’s understanding of the final total.

Treat location and timing as live information

Give users a way to check the delivery address and distinguish an estimate from a confirmed event. If the service cannot provide a precise live location, do not draw a moving marker that implies it can. Explain delays using available information and offer a relevant support path. Good communication is more valuable than decorative progress that is disconnected from the actual operation.

Prepare a focused first release

A first version can serve a limited delivery area and a manageable set of restaurants while still supporting the complete order journey. Avoid expanding coverage before the core handoffs are understood. Test normal orders, unavailable items, cancellations and support escalation. Agree on the operational responsibilities before launch so the product team is not asked to solve an undefined business process with additional screens.

A first version can serve a limited delivery area and a manageable set of restaurants while still supporting the complete order journey.

title: How to evaluate an AI tool for your team
layout:
AI tools

How to evaluate an AI tool for your team

A practical checklist that begins with the work rather than the feature list.

IN THIS ARTICLEDefine the task and the baselineTest representative examplesCount the whole workflowMake adoption a decisionRun a small comparison that can be repeatedExample: evaluate meeting-note assistanceAsk the operating questions earlyChoose an adoption rule

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Define the task and the baseline

Choose one recurring task and describe how it works today. Record the time involved, the required quality and the common mistakes. This gives your trial something to compare against. A tool that feels impressive in a demonstration may add little value to a task your team already completes reliably.

Test representative examples

Include easy cases, messy inputs and requests that should be rejected or escalated. Ask the people doing the work to review the output. Do not rely solely on the person who introduced the tool. Different reviewers may notice missing context, awkward formatting or assumptions that affect the final result.

Count the whole workflow

Include preparation, checking, correction and handoff when judging effort. Consider whether the output moves easily into the systems you already use. Review the data access needed and the responsibilities of the team maintaining it. A faster first draft can still create a slower overall process if cleanup is substantial.

Make adoption a decision

Set a review date and agree on the evidence needed to keep, limit or stop using the tool. Start with a reversible pilot. If a product changes, revisit the relevant assumptions rather than treating your first evaluation as permanent. The goal is a useful working process, not a growing collection of subscriptions.

Run a small comparison that can be repeated

Give each candidate the same task, inputs and review criteria. Remove confidential information unless its use has been authorized and the tool is appropriate for it. Record the output before editing it so you can distinguish the tool’s contribution from the reviewer’s corrections. If one candidate requires substantial setup, count that effort separately. A fair comparison does not mean every product must be used identically, but the final work should meet the same standard.

Example: evaluate meeting-note assistance

Use an approved sample discussion and define the expected output: decisions, owners, deadlines and open questions. Include a point that was proposed but not agreed. The tool should not turn that suggestion into a confirmed task. Ask reviewers to identify missing or invented commitments. Also assess whether the result is easy to edit and share. The best summary is not necessarily the most detailed; it is the one that preserves the distinctions the team relies on.

Ask the operating questions early

Who controls the account, who can access the inputs and where does the output go? Can the team export its work if it changes tools? Who checks a result before it becomes a customer-facing message? These questions affect the workflow even when the trial is small. Write down the answers rather than assuming they will become obvious after purchase. Review current provider documentation and your organization’s requirements before connecting production information.

Choose an adoption rule

A practical decision can be conditional: use the tool for first drafts, retain manual review and exclude a particular sensitive task. You do not need an all-or-nothing verdict. Schedule a review after enough real work has passed through the pilot to reveal common issues. Keep or expand the tool when it improves the complete process. title: Plan your CMS around content, not just pages
layout:

Plan your CMS around content, not just pages

A good content model makes a growing website easier to maintain.

IN THIS ARTICLEIdentify the things you publishAvoid the giant text boxPlan relationships and publishingGive editors a realistic previewExample: model an article libraryDesign the editor’s next actionPrepare for a larger collectionMake the handoff practical

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Identify the things you publish

List the recurring content types: articles, services, projects, people or products. Each type needs a small set of fields that reflect its purpose. An article might need a title, summary, body and topic. A project may need a problem statement, images and a clear description of the work delivered.

Avoid the giant text box

If everything lives in a single freeform field, editors must repeatedly recreate the same structure. Shared fields make consistent rendering easier. At the same time, do not turn every sentence into a separate field. Model the decisions editors need to make, with enough flexibility for meaningful content differences.

Plan relationships and publishing

Decide whether an article can belong to several topics and how related content is selected. Define what a draft means and who can publish. Consider what happens when a project or article is removed. A stable link strategy and a clear editorial workflow prevent growth from becoming a collection of manual fixes.

Give editors a realistic preview

Editors should see how content behaves with a long title, missing image or short summary. Explain required fields and provide useful validation messages. Test the workflow with the people who will use it. A CMS succeeds when publishing accurate content is understandable without relying on the developer for every small change.

Example: model an article library

An article can have a stable slug, title, short description, category, cover image, body, author and publication state. A category should be managed consistently rather than typed differently on every article. Include image credit information where it is needed. Decide whether a changed title should change the URL; often the better editorial experience is to keep the URL stable and manage deliberate redirects separately.

Design the editor’s next action

A writer should understand how to save a draft, preview it and submit it for review. A publisher should see what changed and what remains incomplete. Required fields should explain the problem and how to fix it. Avoid using a technical error message for an ordinary missing title. Test the workflow with an article that has no image and another with several images so the team can see whether the content model supports real publishing needs.

Prepare for a larger collection

As the library grows, editors need search, clear status filters and useful sorting. Readers need relevant topics and predictable navigation. These are related but different interfaces. Decide how archived content is treated and how related articles are selected. A small amount of structure at the beginning prevents a larger collection from turning into duplicate categories, inconsistent cards and pages that are difficult to find.

Make the handoff practical

Provide a short guide covering the everyday editing tasks, image sizes and review process. Have the future editor publish a practice article while you observe where the workflow is confusing. Correct the interface or instructions before handoff. A CMS is not finished because its database can store text; it is ready when the responsible people can publish and maintain accurate content with confidence.

Provide a short guide covering the everyday editing tasks, image sizes and review process.

title: Using Gemini to prototype a useful AI feature
layout:
