Using Gemini to prototype a useful AI feature

Start with a focused task, a realistic sample and a way to judge the output.

IN THIS ARTICLEChoose one job for the modelCreate a small evaluation setDesign the review experiencePlan beyond the demoA worked example: turn a brief into questionsMake the output usable by another personA simple scorecard for the pilotWhat to hand over at the end

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Choose one job for the model

Google’s Gemini API supports generative AI features such as text generation and multimodal input. That creates many possibilities, but a useful prototype begins with one task. For example, try turning a short product brief into a structured list of questions. Define what a good answer contains before choosing the interface. See the official Gemini documentation linked below for supported capabilities.

Source: Gemini API documentation ↗

Create a small evaluation set

Prepare several realistic examples with different levels of detail. Include incomplete input, unfamiliar terminology and requests outside the intended scope. Write down what you expect from each case. Compare generated results against that checklist instead of selecting only the most impressive demonstration. A prototype should reveal where the idea fails as well as where it works.

Design the review experience

Give users an opportunity to edit or reject the result. Show the original input alongside the generated output when comparison matters. If the system cannot complete the task, offer a clear next step. A generic error or a confident but unsupported answer leaves the user doing the product’s recovery work.

Plan beyond the demo

Before launch, assign responsibility for credentials, usage limits, feedback and ongoing evaluation. Decide which data the feature actually needs and avoid sending unrelated customer information. Check current provider documentation when implementing. The prototype proves a possible interaction; it does not establish production reliability or a fixed operating cost.

A worked example: turn a brief into questions

Imagine a founder uploads a short description of a delivery app. Your feature should identify the people involved, separate known requirements from assumptions and propose the five questions that would most affect the estimate. Provide an example brief where the delivery region is missing and another where the region is explicit. A successful result asks about the missing region only in the first case. This is more useful evidence than a fluent paragraph describing a delivery app in general.

Make the output usable by another person

Give each proposed question a reason and connect it to a decision. “Will restaurants manage their own menus?” affects operational roles and screens; “What colors do you like?” belongs to a later design conversation. Keep the result short enough to review and let the founder edit it before sharing. Store the approved version separately from the generated draft so collaborators can tell which decisions are confirmed. Do not treat the model’s suggested requirements as an agreed scope.

A simple scorecard for the pilot

Review whether the output stays within the brief, notices missing information, avoids unsupported commitments and follows the requested structure. Use the same scorecard on every example. Ask a second reviewer to assess a few outputs independently; disagreement often exposes a vague requirement in your evaluation. Record failures in ordinary language. “Invented a payment provider” gives the team something to fix, while “the AI was bad” does not identify the underlying behavior.

What to hand over at the end

Deliver the prototype together with its example inputs, review criteria, known limitations and the decision about whether to continue. Name the person responsible for approving changes to the prompt or connected content. Keep model choice separate from the business goal so the feature can be evaluated again when implementation options change. The strongest next step may be a narrower task, a better input form or a simpler rule-based feature, rather than adding more generative behavior.

title: Why design should come before development
layout:
Product strategy

Why design should come before development

A clearer scope, fewer surprises and a better starting point for your product.

IN THIS ARTICLEStart with the user’s taskMake decisions while changes are inexpensiveDesign enough to guide the buildKeep the conversation goingStart with a small discovery briefExample: simplify a booking journeyReview the states around the happy pathUse approval to create a shared baseline

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Start with the user’s task

A feature list describes what a product contains. A user journey explains what someone needs to accomplish. Before discussing colors or code, map the main task from entry to completion. Identify the information users need at each step.

Make decisions while changes are inexpensive

Wireframes let you compare structures without committing to implementation. A prototype helps you discuss navigation and behavior. This does not eliminate changes during development, but it gives the team a clearer shared reference.

Design enough to guide the build

Not every project needs months of research. A small website may need a clear content structure and responsive layouts. A complex application needs more attention to roles, errors and edge cases. Match the design effort to the uncertainty.

Keep the conversation going

A design file is not the end of collaboration. Designers and developers should review the implementation together, especially around responsive behavior, accessibility and loading states.

Start with a small discovery brief

Write down the audience, their main task, the business outcome and the constraints already known. Keep assumptions separate from confirmed requirements. For example, a founder may believe users need an account before viewing products, but that is a decision to examine rather than a fact. A short brief gives the team a common reference and prevents early conversations from becoming a disconnected collection of favorite screens and visual styles.

Example: simplify a booking journey

Map how someone finds a service, selects a time, provides the necessary details and receives confirmation. Ask what information is required at each step. If the visitor must create a detailed profile before seeing availability, test whether that sequence is necessary. A wireframe lets the team compare alternatives before the development effort is committed. The goal is to resolve meaningful uncertainty, not to produce a large number of intermediate screens.

Review the states around the happy path

Include no availability, invalid input, a failed request and a returning user. These states often reveal requirements hidden by the ideal journey. Discuss them with the developer while the flow is still flexible. Decide which behavior needs confirmation from the business. A handoff that includes the surrounding states is more actionable than a polished sequence where every request succeeds and every field contains perfectly sized content.

Use approval to create a shared baseline

Review the agreed journey, representative screens and remaining questions together. Record what has been approved and what is still open. This does not make the design immutable; it makes later changes easier to discuss. When a new requirement arrives, the team can explain its effect on scope and timing. Design before code creates a clearer starting point for collaboration, not a promise that the project will never need adjustment.

KEY TAKEAWAY

title: How to define a useful first version
layout:
Development

How to define a useful first version

Build around one meaningful user journey before expanding your feature list.

IN THIS ARTICLEChoose one core outcomeSeparate essentials from assumptionsInclude the unglamorous workAgree on a review pointWrite the first-version promiseExample: define what can waitInclude the work behind the screensPlan the first learning cycle

By Muhammad Faraz · 3 min read

Choose one core outcome

Write down the single most important task your first users should complete. A first version should make that task useful from beginning to end, even if the surrounding feature set is limited.

Separate essentials from assumptions

Some features are required for the main workflow. Others express an idea about what users might want later. Keep those assumptions visible so they do not silently become launch requirements.

Include the unglamorous work

Error handling, empty states, permissions and deployment are part of a working product. Discuss them early so the estimate covers more than polished screenshots.

Agree on a review point

Define what you want to learn after the first release. Feedback should help decide the next milestone. Avoid treating the original feature list as a permanent commitment when real usage points in another direction.

Write the first-version promise

Describe the useful outcome a person can complete in the initial release. For a scheduling product, that might be creating a shift, assigning it and confirming availability. Keep the promise specific enough to test. A list of impressive features is not a substitute for an end-to-end outcome. If the proposed scope contains several unrelated promises, consider which one creates the strongest reason for an initial user to try the product.

Example: define what can wait

A scheduling MVP may need basic team access and clear shift status before it needs advanced forecasting. It may need a reliable way to correct an assignment before it needs a decorative analytics dashboard. Explain why each deferred feature can wait without breaking the core journey. This is different from removing difficult work at random. The first version should remain coherent even when the surrounding feature set is deliberately small.

Include the work behind the screens

Account for permissions, data handling, errors, test environments and launch responsibilities in the scope. A screen count alone does not describe the complete effort. Ask the development team which assumptions could materially change the estimate. Resolve the most consequential ones before committing to a fixed milestone. This helps avoid a situation where the visible interface looks complete while essential operational behavior has never been planned.

Plan the first learning cycle

Choose what to observe after release and how that evidence will influence the next milestone. Interview users about the task they attempted, inspect where they needed help and identify workarounds. Keep new requests visible without immediately treating all of them as commitments. A first version is valuable when it helps the team make better decisions about the product, not simply when it reproduces an early idea with fewer screens.

KEY TAKEAWAY

Choose what to observe after release and how that evidence will influence the next milestone.
